passages.t: The word to Hosea, and a command to marry
passages.happening:
The book opens with its heading. This is the word of the LORD that came to Hosea son of Beeri, in the days of four kings of Judah, Uzziah, Jotham, Ahaz and Hezekiah, and of one king of Israel, Jeroboam son of Jehoash (verse 1).

Then comes the first thing the LORD says through him, and it is a shock. He tells Hosea, ‘Go, take a prostitute as your wife and have children of adultery, because this land is flagrantly prostituting itself by departing from the LORD’ (verse 2). Hosea obeys. He marries Gomer daughter of Diblaim, and she conceives and bears him a son (verse 3).
passages.hearers:
The heading places Hosea in the eighth century BC. He began under Jeroboam II of Israel, whose long reign brought wider borders and wealth (2 Kings 14:23-29), and the list of Judah's kings reaches to Hezekiah. So Hosea spoke for decades, from before Jeroboam died, about 753 BC, into the last years of the northern kingdom. The heading names four kings of Judah and only one of Israel. That may be because the book was kept in Judah, or it may quietly pass over the short-lived kings of the north who came after Jeroboam.

The Hebrew behind ‘a prostitute as your wife’ is literally a wife of harlotries. Marriage in ancient Israel was arranged between families, and a husband's honor was bound up with his wife's faithfulness. For a prophet to marry a woman known for sleeping with other men, or one who would become unfaithful, would bring public shame on him. That shame is the point. God is showing what Israel's unfaithfulness has done to him. ‘The land’ here means its people, and its prostitution is the worship of Baal, whom many Israelites thanked for rain and good fields.

The verb in verse 2, zanah, to act as a prostitute, and the words built from it run through the whole book. It is Hosea's main picture for a people who have left their God.
passages.later: Jeremiah and Ezekiel took up the same picture of the LORD's people as an unfaithful wife (Jeremiah 2 to 3; Ezekiel 16 and 23). Other prophets also lived out their message in their homes: Isaiah's sons carried names that were messages too (Isaiah 7:3; 8:3).
passages.hard:
Did God really command a prophet to marry a prostitute?

Readers have been troubled by this from the start, and interpreters take it in several ways. Some hold that Gomer was already known for sleeping with other men, perhaps in the fertility rites of the shrines, and that the command is meant to shock: God has bound himself to a people like that. Others note that the Hebrew says a wife of harlotries, not the ordinary word for a prostitute, and read it as looking ahead. On this view she was faithful when Hosea married her and later strayed, and the story names her by what she became, as Israel was faithful in her youth (2:15) and strayed later. Still others, some medieval Jewish interpreters among them, proposed that the marriage happened in a vision or is a parable. Most modern scholars think the names of Gomer and her father point to a real marriage. These notes do not decide between the readings.

On any of them, Hosea's pain mirrors God's. Scripture does not hold this up as a model to copy. It is a prophetic sign, a picture of God and a nation, in which one man's life carried God's grief. It gives no warrant for any man to shame or harm a wife, and no one may use it to call a woman worthless or to treat her as her husband's to punish.

Nothing in this passage asks anyone to stay where they or their children are in danger. If you are in an abusive marriage, seek safety first. Talk to a pastor or a counselor you trust, or call a local domestic violence line. These notes are not legal advice. The Find Help page on this site lists places to turn.
passages.asks: God calls Israel's worship of other gods adultery, the betrayal of a person and not only the breaking of a rule. Ask how that picture changes the way you think about what you trust most. And ask what it says about God that he chose to make his own grief known in this way.

passages.happening:
The LORD names the first son. ‘Name him Jezreel, for soon I will bring the bloodshed of Jezreel upon the house of Jehu, and I will put an end to the kingdom of Israel’ (verse 4). On that day he will break Israel's bow in the Valley of Jezreel (verse 5).

Gomer conceives again and bears a daughter. The LORD says to name her Lo-ruhamah, which means No Compassion, ‘for I will no longer have compassion on the house of Israel, that I should ever forgive them’ (verse 6). Yet he will have compassion on Judah, and save them ‘not by bow or sword or war, not by horses and cavalry, but by the LORD their God’ (verse 7).

After she weans Lo-ruhamah, Gomer bears another son. ‘Name him Lo-ammi, for you are not My people, and I am not your God’ (verse 9).
passages.hearers:
Names in the ancient Near East were often statements, and prophets sometimes gave their children names that carried a message. Hosea's children became walking sermons. Anyone who asked a child's name heard a verdict on the nation.

Jezreel carried history. It was a royal city and the broad, fertile valley beside it. There, about 841 BC, Jehu, anointed at Elisha's word, killed King Joram of Israel, King Ahaziah of Judah, Queen Jezebel and the whole house of Ahab (2 Kings 9 to 10). Jehu founded the line to which Jeroboam II belonged. That line ended when Jeroboam's son Zechariah was murdered after six months (2 Kings 15:8-12), and the kingdom itself ended some thirty years later.

Lo-ruhamah comes from the word for compassion, which is built on the word for the womb: the tender love of a parent. Lo-ammi turns the covenant words of Sinai inside out. God had said he would be their God and they would be his people. The names grow harsher one by one, from the end of a dynasty, to the end of compassion for the nation, to the covenant itself undone. In the Hebrew, the last line of verse 9 says that God will not be ehyeh to them. Ehyeh, meaning am or will be, is the word God used when he made his name known at the burning bush (Exodus 3:14), and many interpreters hear the covenant name itself withdrawn here. The BSB, like most English Bibles, smooths the line.
passages.later: Jehu had been told, “Four generations of your sons will sit on the throne of Israel” (2 Kings 15:12), and 2 Kings records that word fulfilled when Zechariah died. The words Lo-ammi reverses are the promise of the law: ‘I will walk among you and be your God, and you will be My people’ (Leviticus 26:12).
passages.hard:
Why is Jehu's house judged for the bloodshed of Jezreel, when 2 Kings says God approved what he did?

Second Kings credits Jehu with doing ‘what is right in My sight’ in carrying out judgment on Ahab's house (2 Kings 10:30). Hosea, about a century later, announces judgment for the blood he shed there. Interpreters read this in three main ways, as the notes on 2 Kings 10 also set out. Some think Jehu went beyond his commission, killing with a brutality and for motives of his own that God did not approve. Some think the purge became a political act, and later kings of his line carried its guilt by keeping its sins. Others think 2 Kings and Hosea give two judgments side by side, as Scripture sometimes does: Jehu did what God had said, and he did it in a way that was still bloodguilt.

On any reading, being used by God in a judgment does not make anyone righteous. Jehu's coup gives no one a warrant for violence in God's name.
passages.asks: Each child's name carried a message. Ask what someone would learn about your deepest loyalties from the way you live. And notice verse 7: Judah's rescue would come not by bow or sword but by the LORD. Ask what you are counting on to keep you safe.

passages.happening:
Then, with no warning, the chapter turns. ‘Yet the number of the Israelites will be like the sand of the sea, which cannot be measured or counted’ (verse 10). In the very place where they were told they were not God's people, they will be called sons of the living God.

The people of Judah and of Israel will be gathered together. They will appoint one leader for themselves and go up out of the land. ‘For great will be the day of Jezreel’ (verse 11).
passages.hearers:
These two verses reverse every name. Not My People becomes sons of the living God. The scattered are gathered. Jezreel means God sows, and the name that recalled a massacre becomes the name of a great day of planting. The north and the south, divided for two centuries, become one people again under one leader. Hosea will soon tie that leader to David's line (3:5).

The promise reaches back to God's word to Abraham and to Jacob about descendants as many as the sand. Judgment is real, but God's promises to Abraham outlast Israel's unfaithfulness.

In many Hebrew Bibles these two verses are numbered 2:1-2, so the promise opens the next chapter. English Bibles place it here, at the end of the bad news.
passages.later: God promised Abraham descendants as many as ‘the sand on the seashore’ (Genesis 22:17). Paul quotes these verses to show God's mercy now reaching Gentiles as well as Jews: “It will happen that in the very place where it was said to them” (Romans 9:26), they will be called the children of the living God. Peter tells scattered believers, ‘Once you were not a people, but now you are the people of God’ (1 Peter 2:10).
passages.asks: The chapter moves from Not My People to children of the living God. Ask where you have seen God bring hope out of what looked like only judgment. And ask whether you have ever counted yourself among those God could not want, and what these verses say to that.
